one_liner: Native OxCaml simdjson port: reusable tape mode 1.18x RapidJSON geomean; DOM mode 0.69x RapidJSON, 4.9x Yojson.
what_it_does: A JSON parser written in OxCaml (Jane Street's OCaml fork with SIMD and unboxed types) that reimplements simdjson's algorithms natively rather than binding to the C++ library. The main API, `Simdjson.parse : string -> (Json.t, parse_error) result`, returns its own DOM type (`Int of int`, `Float of float#`, `Object of assoc array`, `Array of t array`), and a reusable `Simdjson.Parser` amortizes buffer allocation across parses. An experimental `Simdjson.Tape` module produces a simdjson-style packed int64 tape, either owned or borrowed from a reusable `Tape.Parser`. It only parses: there is no serializer and no On-Demand or streaming API.
how_it_is_fast: Stage 1 follows simdjson's structural indexing on 64-byte blocks (four SSE 16-byte vectors): nibble lookup tables (PSHUFB) classify bytes, simdjson's backslash-run subtraction trick finds escapes, a carry-less-multiply prefix-XOR builds in-string masks, and the lookup-4 algorithm validates UTF-8. Structural positions stay compressed as one 64-bit mask per 64 input bytes, which stage 2, a tail-recursive descent, walks with count-trailing-zeros while writing either the `Json.t` tree or a tape whose strings share one byte buffer, so the reusable tape path allocates zero OCaml words per parse. Numbers use an 8-digit SWAR batch and a native port of Lemire's fast_float (Clinger fast path plus a 64x64->128 multiply lowered to one x86 `mul`), with a strtod fallback. OxCaml's unboxed `int64#`/`float#`, `[@zero_alloc]` checks and `[@@builtin]` popcnt/ctz intrinsics keep the hot loops free of boxing.
when_to_use: An OCaml service on x86-64 where Yojson or Jsont parsing is the bottleneck. On 100 KB-3 MB documents the DOM mode measured about 4.9x Yojson.Safe and 5.4x Jsont (geomean).
Hot loops that parse many documents and can consume each result right away. The reusable `Tape.Parser` allocates nothing in steady state and was the fastest OCaml mode at 1,248 MB/s geomean.
Object- and string-heavy JSON (API logs, catalogs, tweets). Tape mode beat RapidJSON on apache_builds, citm_catalog, gsoc-2018 and twitter.
Teams already on OxCaml who want SIMD parsing without C++ FFI. The only C code is a tiny linker stub.
when_not_to_use: Stock OCaml. It needs the OxCaml 5.2.0+ox compiler and Jane Street's `ocaml_simd`, and will not build on upstream OCaml.
ARM (Apple Silicon, Graviton). The SIMD code is x86 SSE only, there is no runtime CPU dispatch, and there is no AVX2 path yet.

Float-heavy documents such as GeoJSON or numeric arrays, if you hoped to beat RapidJSON. Tape mode lost to it on canada, marine_ik and numbers. In the DOM path the author measured about 42% of cycles going to GC/promotion on canada.json.
Cases that need error positions or messages, serialization, lazy On-Demand access, or exact integers beyond 63 bits.
Untrusted or deeply nested input in production. The parser has no nesting-depth limit, it is a single-author project with 3 stars and no releases, and it has no issue history to learn from.

integration.form: module (dune library `simdjson`, built from source; no tags or releases, and the generated opam file still has placeholder homepage and dev-repo URLs, so expect to pin from git)
integration.dependencies: ocaml_simd (sse, avx, ppx, sexp sublibraries), janestreet_shims, base, stdlib_upstream_compatible, ppx_expect and ppx_template (preprocess); one C stub file
integration.min_toolchain: OxCaml 5.2.0+ox (the setup script pins an OxCaml opam-repository commit), Dune 3.22
integration.platforms: x86-64 only. It uses SSE 128-bit vectors with PSHUFB lookups and a carry-less multiply; the exact minimum ISA is not documented. No ARM, and no AVX2 dispatch yet.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. `Parser.t` and `Tape.Parser.t` own mutable buffers that are reused across calls, so use one per domain (inferred from the API). The one-shot `Simdjson.parse` creates its own buffers on every call.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false. RapidJSON is a C++ library. Within OCaml the result is a new `Json.t` AST, not Yojson's polymorphic variants, and there is no printer.

gotchas: The tape returned by `Tape.Parser.parse` borrows the parser's buffers, in simdjson's `dom::parser` style. The next `parse` on that parser overwrites it. Use `Tape.parse` or `Tape.to_json` if you need to keep the result.
Integers are 63-bit OCaml ints. Values beyond that but within the int64/uint64 range come back silently as `Float`, which loses precision. Larger integers are rejected as `Invalid_json`.

Every parse failure is the single `Error Invalid_json`, with no position or category. Unimplemented paths and internal defects raise `Internal_error` instead. Stage 2 is recursive, and the design notes say pathologically nested input can overflow the native stack.
Tape format limits: strings are capped at 16 MB (24-bit length), string offsets and container end indexes are 32-bit packed fields, and container element counts saturate at 24 bits.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you must stay in OCaml/OxCaml with no C++ FFI. In the same run C++ simdjson was about 2.7x faster than its best mode and sajson about 1.3x faster. For C/C++, or where bindings are acceptable, simdjson or yyjson is the better choice. simd-json (Rust) and simdjson-go are the equivalent ports for other languages.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran one benchmark on 2026-08-15: an i7-12700K pinned to one P-core, with the OxCaml 5.2.0+ox perf profile against C++ parsers built by GCC 15.2.1 in CMake Release under Google Benchmark. On 7 simdjson-data fixtures, the reusable tape mode averaged 1,247.7 MB/s geomean against RapidJSON DOM's 1,059.7 MB/s (about 1.18x) and won 4 of 7. The recommended DOM API reached 729.5 MB/s (about 0.69x RapidJSON), and C++ simdjson reached 3,344.5 MB/s. RapidJSON was run with default parse flags and a fresh Document per iteration, and was built without RAPIDJSON_SSE2/SSE42 or -march flags.
status_note: Actively developed by a single author (last commit 2026-08-23) and MIT-licensed. It is usable today by pinning the git repo into an OxCaml switch, but it has no releases and the author describes the tape API as experimental.
